damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Film Scene 21 (courtyard, Neville steps forward toward Voldemort with Sorting Hat)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Neville is singled out by Voldemort after being identified as the boy who gave the Carrows trouble. Voldemort recruits him, Neville flatly refuses ('I'll join you when hell freezes over'), shouts 'Dumbledore's Army!' to rally the crowd, and is then forcibly placed under the Body-Bind Curse with a burning Sorting Hat as punishment. His defiance is unambiguous and immediate — he never appears to be surrendering.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film stages Neville walking forward voluntarily toward Voldemort with his chin on his chest and his gaze to the ground, so that onlookers (Seamus included) and the audience read it as surrender or collaboration. He is treated with derision ('the best Hogwarts has to offer?'). The framing creates deliberate ambiguity about his intent that does not exist in the book, and removes the spontaneous, defiant rallying cry ('Dumbledore's Army!') that motivates the crowd.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Neville is immediately, loudly defiant — his refusal is the spark that emboldens the survivors. The film undercuts this by visually coding his approach as possible capitulation, delaying the reveal of his intent and stripping the crowd-rallying 'Dumbledore's Army!' shout entirely. His courage reads as a twist rather than a character expression, and the moment loses its function as collective inspiration.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Film Scene 22 (courtyard, Neville's speech to the crowd)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book gives Neville no extended speech. His defiance is a single blunt line ('I'll join you when hell freezes over') followed by a rallying cry. The moment is brief, sharp, and visceral — consistent with his established voice throughout DH: understated, matter-of-fact courage.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film gives Neville a scripted inspirational monologue ('People die every day... they didn't die in vain... Harry's heart did beat for us') culminating in spitting at Voldemort. The voice is oratorical and sentimental, quite unlike his terse, dry characterisation elsewhere in both corpora.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The speech imposes a generic hero-rallying register onto a character whose entire book appeal is that his bravery is expressed without rhetoric. The book corpus consistently shows Neville speaking matter-of-factly about horrific things ('Doesn't matter. They don't want to spill too much pure blood'). The film speech is out of voice and softens the starkness that makes his courage distinctive.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Film Scene 23 (entrance hall, Neville steps between Harry and Voldemort and is blasted away)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Neville kills Nagini in a single decisive moment immediately after breaking free of the Body-Bind, drawing the sword from the Sorting Hat in one fluid motion during the chaos of the centaurs' charge. The act is his alone, executed with agency and precise timing. He is not incapacitated before killing the snake.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film splits the sword-drawing and the snake-killing into two separate scenes. In the first (Scene 23), Neville draws the sword but is immediately blasted fifty feet across the hall by Voldemort's spell before he can use it, and the narrative frames this as potentially fatal ('no one could have survived that'). The snake-kill is then completed later (Scene 25) almost incidentally, after Neville recovers off-screen.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's snake-kill is a single climactic flourish of agency: Neville breaks free, draws the sword, and kills Nagini in one unbroken movement. The film fractures this into a failed heroic attempt followed by a later clean-up action, removing the dramatic unity. The interposition of Neville being blasted nearly to death also introduces a survival-spectacle beat that overshadows the killing itself, and the snake-kill in Scene 25 arrives almost as an afterthought while Harry and Voldemort are the main focus.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Film Scene 15 (marble staircase, Neville tells Harry he is 'mad for Luna')
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes no romantic interest between Neville and Luna. Luna's ceiling portrait (book Scene 15-16) shows she treasures Neville as a friend, linked by the word 'friends' repeated in gold. The book corpus contains no hint of Neville having feelings for Luna.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Neville announces mid-battle, 'I'm mad for her! Think it's about time I told her, seeing as there's a pretty good chance we'll both be dead by dawn!' This is played for light comic relief.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film invents a romantic sub-plot for Neville with no book basis. While brief, it is confirmed by the film's epilogue staging (Scene 26: Luna sits down close beside Neville and smiles). This reframes a friendship-based relationship and attaches a romantic-comedy beat to a character whose arc is about courage and resilience, not romance. It also implicitly reduces Luna's independent characterisation.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Film Scene 26 (Great Hall epilogue, Luna sits beside Neville)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book epilogue (Scene 181) shows Neville surrounded by 'a knot of fervent admirers' with the sword of Gryffindor beside his plate — he is celebrated for his heroism in his own right. Luna is not mentioned in his immediate company.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Luna sits close beside Neville and smiles at him in a manner that confirms the romantic framing established in Scene 15, replacing the book's image of Neville as an independently celebrated hero with a romantic-resolution tableau.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book closes Neville's arc with him as a figure of admiration in his own right. The film closes it with a romantic beat that subordinates his heroic resolution to a relationship pay-off the books never establish, slightly deflecting attention from his individual arc completion.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Film Scene 17 (entrance hall, Neville and Oliver Wood carry Nigel's body)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 133-135 shows Neville carrying Colin Creevey's body in from the grounds. The moment is explicitly weighted: Colin was underage, he sneaked back, and 'he was tiny in death.' Neville hands the body to Oliver Wood and then returns to the darkness to recover more bodies — he 'looked like an old man.' This is a defining beat of Neville's wartime gravity and quiet service.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film replaces Colin Creevey with 'Nigel,' a minor invented film character, stripping the scene of its emotional and thematic weight. The specific pathos of an underage boy who sneaked back to fight — resonant with Neville's own arc of unrecognised sacrifice — is lost.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The substitution of Nigel for Colin removes the specific poignancy the book attaches to this beat. Colin is a character the audience has known since year two; his death and Neville's quiet service in recovering him is a moment of real weight. Replacing him with a generic film-original character drains the scene of its resonance and diminishes Neville's role as a witness and caretaker of the war's cost.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Film Scenes 4-7 (passage and Room of Requirement — absence of Neville's full resistance narrative)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book passage (Scenes 37-83) gives Neville an extended account of the year: the DA's graffiti campaigns, losing Luna at Christmas and Ginny after Easter, Michael Corner being tortured, the Carrows failing to break him, his grandmother being targeted, Dawlish being hospitalised by Gran, Gran's letter saying he is his parents' son, and his consequent decision to disappear into the Room of Requirement. This narrative establishes him as the primary resistance leader at Hogwarts during Harry's absence, with a fully realised arc of escalating stakes and personal cost.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film condenses this to a brief exchange in the passage (Scene 5) covering only the Carrows' punishments and the gash on Neville's face. The year-long resistance campaign, the loss of Luna and Ginny as co-leaders, the DA's communications network, his grandmother's defiance, and the personal cost to Neville are all absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The missing material is not incidental colour — it is the substance of Neville's arc across Deathly Hallows. Without it, the film's Neville arrives battered but without context for why or at what cost, and the audience cannot appreciate the scale of what he has led and endured. His climactic moments (the speech, the sword) therefore lack the earned foundation the book provides. This is the single largest source of structural damage to the characterisation.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Film Scene 7 (Room of Requirement — Neville's challenge to Harry about trust and fighting together)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 91-113 show Neville pressing Harry directly and with genuine moral weight: 'We're his army... We were all in it together... I don't see why you can't trust us. Everyone in this room's proven they're loyal.' He speaks with earned authority as the year's resistance leader, and his frustration is principled, not merely emotional. He also takes the initiative of calling Luna and Ginny back via the fake Galleons.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film collapses this exchange. Neville asks 'What's the plan, Harry?' and accepts Harry's vague answer without the sustained, principled challenge of the book. The moral tension — Neville's legitimate claim that the DA has fought and bled and deserves to know why they are being excluded — is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book exchange is one of the few moments where Neville speaks to Harry as a moral equal and actually challenges him. It reflects his growth into a leader who has earned the right to demand accountability. Removing it reduces Neville to a supportive secondary character and weakens the peer dynamic between him and Harry at the story's climax.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Film Scenes 18-20 (courtyard before Voldemort's ultimatum — absence of Harry's private conversation with Neville about Nagini)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 137-156 show Harry seeking Neville out deliberately, pulling off the Invisibility Cloak to ensure Neville sees him, lying to protect him ('Course not... this is something else'), and entrusting him with the Horcrux secret as a backup: 'Dumbledore had died knowing that three people still knew about the Horcruxes; now Neville would take Harry's place.' Neville grips Harry's wrist and says 'We're all going to keep fighting, Harry. You know that?' — and pats him on the shoulder before returning to recover bodies. This is Harry consciously choosing Neville as his heir to the secret.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene is absent from the film entirely. The Nagini instruction reaches Neville only incidentally — he overhears Harry shouting 'The snake! We've got to kill the snake!' in Scene 23. There is no private moment, no deliberate trust, no Harry choosing Neville.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book scene is the moment Harry formally passes responsibility to Neville, cementing their relationship as something beyond acquaintance. It gives Neville's snake-kill an intentional, entrusted quality — he kills Nagini because Harry asked him to, privately, as the person Harry most trusts with this. The film's accidental overhearing replaces deliberate trust with proximity, fundamentally changing the meaning of the act and the depth of the Harry-Neville relationship.

main_damage_causes: Wholesale compression of Neville's year-long resistance arc at Hogwarts removes the earned foundation for his climactic moments, leaving his bravery impressive but contextually hollow

The film's staging of the Voldemort confrontation as ambiguous surrender followed by a scripted inspirational speech replaces the book's immediate, understated defiance with a theatrical-hero template that misrepresents his voice and character

The private Harry-Neville conversation — in which Harry deliberately entrusts Neville with the Horcrux secret and the Nagini mission — is entirely absent, replacing a meaningful relationship beat and intentional agency with accidental proximity
